title: Export documentation & customs
sceneDesc: Four illustrated stations show the paper journey that runs alongside the container: shipping instructions, draft Bill of Lading check, export declaration and customs release. The container moves from station to station.

narration.1: While I was on the road, my data travelled too. The shipper sends the carrier its [[si|shipping instructions]]: who sends, who receives, what's inside me, seal and weights.
narration.2: The [[si]] arrives before the SI cut-off ({siCutoff}): shipper, consignee (or 'to order'), [[notify-party]], description, [[hs-code|HS code]], packages, weights, seal, B/L type and freight terms. [TO VERIFY:v46]
narration.3: SI completeness drives everything downstream: B/L, manifest, ENS. Vague descriptions ('general cargo', 'FAK') are rejected by advance-filing regimes such as ICS2. [TO VERIFY:v23]

caption.2: Consignee 'to order' → [[negotiable-bl|negotiable B/L]]; named consignee, no bank → [[sea-waybill]] possible.

narration.1: The carrier sends back a draft Bill of Lading for checking. Checking now is free; correcting the final B/L is not.
narration.2: Documentation issues the [[draft-bl|draft B/L]]. The shipper must check it before issuance — amendments after issuance cost money. [TO VERIFY:v47]
narration.3: Draft approval: if the shipper doesn't answer by the deadline, many carriers issue as drafted. One field below is inconsistent — find it. [TO VERIFY:v47]

narration.1: Now customs. A [[customs-broker]] files an [[export-declaration]] for the exporter: what the goods are, their value and where they go.
narration.2: The exporter's broker lodges the [[export-declaration]] with invoice, packing list and HS codes. For sea exports, customs often matches it with the terminal's arrival data. [TO VERIFY:v45]
narration.3: Declarant = exporter (or broker under mandate). Liability for the declared data stays largely with the exporter. Under {incoterm}, export clearance: {exportBy}. [TO VERIFY:v45]

caption.2: Under {incoterm}, export clearance is done by the {exportBy}.

narration.1: Customs decides: most containers get a green light without being opened. The release goes to the terminal electronically — no release, no loading.
narration.2: Risk assessment → electronic release to the terminal, or selection for inspection. The carrier files its [[manifest]] and, for the EU, the [[ens]] under [[ics2]] before loading. [TO VERIFY:v23]
narration.3: ICS2: ENS at least 24 h before loading at the foreign port for deep-sea containers; house-level data may come from the NVOCC. A 'do not load' message is binding. [TO VERIFY:v23] [TO VERIFY:v48]
ICS2 returns a 'do not load' message for your box: the goods description in the ENS reads 'general cargo'. The vessel loads in 30 hours.

text.1: An original 'to order' Bill of Lading works like a cheque for the goods: whoever lawfully holds it can claim the cargo.
text.2: Electronic B/Ls are catching up: laws such as the UK Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023 recognise them. [TO VERIFY:v49]

body.2: The SI is the shipper's instruction for the B/L: parties, description, HS code, packages, weights, seal, B/L type, freight terms, originals. Sent by portal, EDI (IFTMIN) or platform before the SI cut-off. [TO VERIFY:v46]
body.3: Common SI errors: consignee vs notify confusion, description too vague for ICS2, seal not updated after inspection, weight inconsistent with VGM. Each one costs an amendment or a hold. [TO VERIFY:v12]

body.1: The [[bl|Bill of Lading]] is the carrier's receipt for the goods and the contract of carriage. An original 'to order' B/L also gives the right to collect the goods at destination.
A specialist who files customs declarations for companies.
body.2: Licensed declarant acting under the exporter's mandate; responsibility for the data largely stays with the exporter. [TO VERIFY:v45]

body.1: Customs checks the data and gives a green light — the 'release'. Without it, the terminal won't load me. Under {incoterm}, export customs is handled by the {exportBy}.
Europe wants to know what's coming before the ship even leaves — for security.
body.2: ICS2: ENS due at least 24 h before loading at the foreign port for deep-sea containerised cargo; the carrier files. [TO VERIFY:v23]

rows.label: Consignee
rows.value: To order of Demo Trade Bank (fictional)

1.2: B/L shipper — also the VGM party. Under {incoterm}: {vgmBy}.

2.2: 'To order of [bank]' → negotiable B/L, transferable by endorsement; used with letters of credit. A named consignee marked non-negotiable → straight B/L or sea waybill.

3.2: STC = 'said to contain': the carrier didn't see inside. The description and HS code should be consistent with the customs declaration and precise enough for ICS2. [TO VERIFY:v46]

40FR.prompt: One field is inconsistent with what you know from step 2 (the B/L gross weight excludes the tare). Tap it.
40FR.explain: The B/L gross weight is the cargo weight ({cargoKg} kg); the VGM adds the tare ({vgm} kg). Corrected before issuance: no amendment fee. [TO VERIFY:v12]

*.prompt: One field doesn't match the seal on the door ({sealNo}). Tap it.
*.explain: Seal on the door {sealNo} vs {wrongSeal} on the draft. Seal mismatches trigger customs and terminal checks and L/C discrepancies. Corrected before issuance: no amendment fee. [TO VERIFY:v12]

value.*: Demo Customs Brokers, for the exporter (fictional)

1.2: The declarant files for the exporter. Under EXW the buyer must arrange it — often impractical abroad. [TO VERIFY:v14]

2.2: The HS code drives export controls and statistics; the description must match the SI and invoice. [TO VERIFY:v46]

3.2: Customs links the declaration to the container and vessel, and often to the terminal's arrival report, before releasing. [TO VERIFY:v45]

E.prompt: Under EXW, who must lodge this export declaration?

options.text: The buyer (through a broker in the export country)
The seller
options.fb: Under EXW the seller only assists, at the buyer's request and cost.

options.text: The carrier
options.fb: The carrier is never the exporter's declarant by default.

options.text: The terminal
options.fb: The terminal reports arrivals; it doesn't declare goods.

E.explain: EXW puts export clearance on the buyer — a common trap; ICC suggests FCA instead. [TO VERIFY:v14]

*.prompt: Under {incoterm}, who must lodge this export declaration?

options.text: The seller (exporter), usually through its customs broker
The buyer
options.fb: Only under EXW does the buyer handle export clearance.

options.text: The carrier
options.fb: The carrier files manifests and ENS, not the export declaration.

options.text: The terminal
options.fb: The terminal reports arrivals; it doesn't declare goods.

*.explain: In every rule except EXW, export clearance is the seller's obligation. [TO VERIFY:v14]

3.prompt: The export declaration describes 'electric appliances, HS 8516' while the SI says 'spare parts'. What's the risk?

options.text: Inconsistent data across declaration, SI/B/L and ENS → holds, inspection, possible penalties
None — customs only reads the declaration
options.fb: Customs and ICS2 cross-check data sources.

options.text: Only a B/L amendment fee
options.fb: The fee is the least of it; the box can be held.

options.text: The Incoterm changes automatically
options.fb: Data errors don't touch the sales contract.

3.explain: Align descriptions and HS codes across all filings before the cut-offs. [TO VERIFY:v45] [TO VERIFY:v23]

documents: **B/L types** — negotiable 'to order', straight, sea waybill, express release, eB/L. [TO VERIFY:v49]
**Manifest**, **ICS2 ENS**; certificate of origin where needed.
costs: **B/L / documentation fee**, **late SI fee**, **amendment fee** after issuance. [TO VERIFY:v12]
**ENS / advance filing fee** at some carriers. [TO VERIFY:v48]
risks: **SI after the cut-off** → late fee, possible shut-out. [TO VERIFY:v12]
**Wrong HS code or vague description** → hold, penalties, L/C discrepancy.
**Misdeclared dangerous goods** → serious safety risk and heavy penalties. [TO VERIFY:v25]
**Missing or wrong ENS** → 'do not load'. [TO VERIFY:v48]
jobs: **Documentation** — SI validation, drafts, B/L issuance, amendments.
**Customs & compliance** — manifests, ICS2, sanctions screening. [TO VERIFY:v48]
**Finance / credit control** — prepaid freight before release of originals. [TO VERIFY:v33]

incoNote.E: Under EXW the buyer must handle export customs — a common trap: the seller holds the documents the buyer needs.
incoNote.F: The seller clears export; the B/L comes from the carrier the buyer booked. FCA allows an agreed on-board B/L to the seller. [TO VERIFY:v14]
incoNote.C: The seller clears export and must give the buyer the transport document (and the insurance document under CIF/CIP). [TO VERIFY:v18]
incoNote.D: The seller clears export; import is for the buyer (DAP/DPU) or the seller (DDP).

1: A container travels twice: physically, and as data.
The shipping instructions become the Bill of Lading — check the draft carefully.
Customs must release the export before loading; most boxes are released without being opened.
2: SI → draft B/L → approval → issuance; amendments after issuance cost money.
B/L type matters: negotiable 'to order', straight, sea waybill, express release or eB/L.
Export clearance follows the Incoterm (EXW = the buyer!); release is electronic and risk-based.
Advance filings such as the EU ICS2 ENS are due before loading at origin.
3: Data must be consistent across SI, B/L, export declaration and ENS.
ICS2 'do not load' is binding: fix the data and refile, or roll the box.
Never issue or date a B/L to fit commercial deadlines.

1.prompt: My papers are sent and customs is on it. I'm at the terminal gate. What happens next?
1.hint: The ship isn't here yet. Where do containers wait at a port?

options.text: I pass the terminal gate: number, seal and condition are checked, then I'm stacked in the yard to wait for my ship.
options.confirm: That's it! The terminal checks that I'm expected, my seal is intact and my condition is fine. Then I wait in the export yard — and my detention clock usually stops here.

options.text: The original Bill of Lading is handed to the truck driver so it travels with me.
options.why: The B/L doesn't travel with the container; originals go to the shipper, often through banks, to the buyer.
options.realLife: An original lost with a driver would be serious: originals are needed to collect the goods.

options.text: I wait outside the port until my ship arrives, then drive straight to it.
options.why: Ships are loaded according to a plan made in advance, so boxes arrive days before.
options.realLife: Arriving at the last minute means missing the cut-off — and the ship.
options.whenRight: Some special cargo goes directly alongside, by prior agreement.

2.prompt: SI in, draft approved, export declaration lodged, ENS filed. The box is at the gate before {cyCutoff}. What happens next?

options.text: Gate-in: pre-advice match, container number, seal and damage check (EIR), VGM status; the box is stacked in the export yard.
options.confirm: Correct. Gate-in is the custody handover to the terminal acting for the carrier. Export detention typically stops here. [TO VERIFY:v21]

options.text: The carrier issues the shipped-on-board B/L now that SI, VGM and customs are in order.
options.why: 'Shipped on board' certifies the box is loaded — it's still at the gate.
options.realLife: An early on-board B/L is a false statement: L/C fraud exposure.
options.whenRight: A 'received for shipment' B/L can be issued after receipt and annotated on board later. [TO VERIFY:v50]

options.text: Direct delivery to the ship's side when the ship berths.
options.why: Standard boxes are received into the yard before the cut-off so the stowage plan can be built.
options.realLife: Turning up at berthing time = missing the CY cut-off = shut-out.
options.whenRight: Some OOG or DG cargo by arrangement. [TO VERIFY:v51]

options.text: The box waits outside until the customs release arrives; terminals only accept released export boxes.
options.why: In many ports the release can follow gate-in: the terminal blocks loading, not entry.
options.realLife: Waiting outside costs truck time and risks the cut-off for nothing.
options.whenRight: Some ports do require an export reference before gate-in. [TO VERIFY:v52]

3.prompt: Case: ICS2 'do not load' because the ENS says 'general cargo'. Loading in 30 hours. What do you do?

options.text: Block the box from loading, get a precise description (and HS code) from the shipper or NVOCC, amend and refile the ENS; if not resolved in time, roll the box.
options.confirm: Right. 'Do not load' is binding. Precise goods descriptions are required; once refiled and cleared, the box can load — otherwise it waits for the next sailing. [TO VERIFY:v23] [TO VERIFY:v48]

options.text: Load anyway; correct the ENS after departure.
options.why: Loading against a 'do not load' breaches EU requirements.
options.realLife: Penalties for the carrier and the box can be refused entry at destination.

options.text: Ask the terminal to override the message.
options.why: The terminal has no authority over EU customs decisions.
options.realLife: No terminal will take that liability.

options.text: Change the description yourself to 'household appliances' so it passes.
options.why: The carrier can't invent cargo data; it must come from the party that knows the goods.
options.realLife: A false declaration makes the carrier liable for misdeclaration.
options.whenRight: Never without the shipper's confirmed data.
